title: Parts of Speech (Word Classes)
summary: Every word class you need for Checkpoint 6: nouns (including abstract nouns), pronouns (including relative pronouns), verbs, modal verbs and infinitives, adjectives, adverbs, determiners, prepositions and conjunctions, how to name a word class in context, and practice with answers.

blocks.text: Every word in a sentence has a job. The job a word does is called its **word class** (another name is **part of speech**). Nouns name things, verbs show actions, adjectives describe nouns, and so on.

Checkpoint reading papers ask about word classes directly. You may be asked: *What word class is the word 'quietly' in this sentence?*, *Find a relative pronoun in paragraph 2*, *Find an abstract noun*, or *Copy an infinitive from the text*. These are quick 1-mark questions, but only if you know the names **exactly**. Word classes also help your writing: strong verbs, precise adjectives and well-placed adverbs earn Vocabulary marks.

blocks.title: Grammar words you must know
items: **Word class / part of speech:** the job a word does in a sentence.
**In context:** in this sentence, in this text. The same word can belong to different classes in different sentences.
**Identify:** find and name it.
**Copy:** write the word exactly as it is in the text.

blocks.text: The word classes at a glance

rows: names a person, place, thing, animal, feeling or idea
takes the place of a noun
shows an action, a state or what is happening
tells us more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb (how, when, where, how often, how much)
comes before a noun and tells us which one or how many
a, an, the, this, my, some, every, three
shows where, when or how something is in relation to something else
and, but, so, because, although, when

blocks.text: 1. Nouns

A **noun** is a naming word. It names a person, a place, a thing, an animal, a feeling or an idea. A quick test: can you put **the** or **a** in front of it? (the castle, a friend, the idea). Names of people and places (proper nouns) are nouns too, even though we do not usually put *a* in front of them.

rows: a general name, with no capital letter
the name of a particular person, place, day, month or organisation, always a capital letter
Nour, Egypt, the Nile, Monday, March
something you can see, touch, hear, smell or taste
a feeling, idea or quality that you **cannot** touch or see
fear, kindness, freedom, honesty, excitement, friendship
team, flock (of birds), herd (of cattle), crowd, class
you can count it, and it has a plural
one pen, two pens / a child, three children
you cannot count it, and it usually has no plural
two words joined to make one noun

blocks.text: **Abstract nouns** are asked about often. Many are made from adjectives or verbs with endings such as **-ness, -ment, -ship, -dom, -ity, -tion, -ance**:

blocks.title: Quick test for an abstract noun
blocks.text: Ask: **Could I put it in a box?** You can put a pencil in a box, so *pencil* is concrete. You cannot put *hope*, *anger* or *success* in a box, so they are abstract. But careful: an abstract noun is still a **noun**. In "She felt **brave**", *brave* is an adjective. In "Her **bravery** surprised us", *bravery* is an abstract noun.
**Plurals.** Most nouns add -s or -es (books, boxes). Some are **irregular**: child → children, man → men, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice, foot → feet, person → people.
2. Pronouns
A **pronoun** replaces a noun so that we do not repeat it. *Salma lost Salma's bag* sounds strange; *Salma lost **her** bag* is better.

rows: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
me, you, him, her, it, us, them
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves
The boy **who** won the race is my cousin.

blocks.text: **Relative pronouns** are very important for Checkpoint. A relative pronoun begins a **relative clause**, which gives more information about a noun that comes just before it:

items: **who** is for people: *My grandfather, **who** is eighty, still walks every day.*
**which** is for things and animals: *The parcel, **which** arrived this morning, was for Dad.*
**that** is for people or things: *This is the book **that** I told you about.*
**whose** shows belonging: *That is the girl **whose** kite got stuck in the tree.*
**whom** is a formal object form of who: *the man to **whom** I spoke*.

blocks.text: You will also see **where** and **when** used in the same way to start a relative clause about a place or a time: *the village **where** my mother was born*, *the day **when** we moved house*.

blocks.title: Trap: 'who', 'which' and 'that' are not always relative pronouns
items: "**Who** broke the vase?" Here *who* asks a question, so it is an **interrogative** pronoun.
"**Which** cake do you want?" Here *which* asks a question before a noun.
"She said **that** she was tired." Here *that* is a conjunction: it joins the reported words to *She said*, and it does not describe a noun.
"**That** bag is heavy." Here *that* points to a noun, so it is a **determiner**.
It is a relative pronoun only when it comes **after a noun** and starts extra information **about that noun**.

blocks.text: 3. Verbs
A **verb** shows what someone or something **does**, **is** or **has**. Every sentence needs at least one verb. Test: can you change its tense? (*I jump → I jumped*.)

rows: show an action you can do or think
link the subject to a word that describes it
be (am, is, are, was, were), seem, become, look, feel
help the main verb to make a tense or a question
be, have, do: *She **is** reading. They **have** finished. **Do** you agree?*
show how possible, necessary or certain something is (they come before another verb)
can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would

blocks.text: **Modal verbs** often appear in persuasive writing and in reading questions about the writer's purpose:

rows: advice: it is a good idea
Anyone **can** join the club. It **could** rain later.
it is possible but not certain
future, certainty or a polite request
I **will** help. **Would** you open the door?

blocks.text: **The infinitive** is the basic form of a verb, usually with **to** in front: *to run, to be, to discover, to help*. Checkpoint can ask you to find or copy an infinitive. Example: *She wanted **to win** the race.* The infinitive often shows **purpose** (why someone does something): *He saved his money **to buy** a bicycle.*

blocks.title: Infinitive or preposition?
blocks.text: **to + verb** = infinitive (*to swim, to explore*). **to + noun** = preposition (*to the beach, to school*). So in "We went **to** the market **to buy** fruit", the first *to* is a preposition and *to buy* is an infinitive.
**Other verb forms you will meet:**

items: **Regular verbs** add -ed in the past: walk → walked, play → played.
**Irregular verbs** change in their own way: go → went → gone, see → saw → seen, write → wrote → written.
**-ing form** (present participle): *running, laughing*. It makes continuous tenses: *They were laughing*.
**Past participle**: *broken, taken, painted*. It is used in the perfect (*has eaten*) and the passive (*The window was broken*).

blocks.text: 4. Adjectives

An **adjective** describes a noun. It tells us what kind, what colour, what size, what something is like. It usually comes **before** the noun (*a **narrow** street*) or **after a linking verb** (*The street was **narrow**.*).

rows: taller, faster, more beautiful, better, worse
tallest, fastest, most beautiful, best, worst

blocks.text: **Rule for comparatives:** short adjectives add **-er/-est** (big → bigger → biggest). Longer adjectives use **more/most** (careful → more careful → most careful). Some are irregular: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst. Never write *more bigger*.
Why does a writer use a comparative? To **compare** two things and show the difference clearly: *The new library is **larger and brighter** than the old one* shows how much better the new one is.
5. Adverbs

An **adverb** tells us more about a verb (how, when, where, how often), or about an adjective or another adverb (how much). Many adverbs end in **-ly**, but many important ones do not: *soon, often, never, very, here, well, fast*.

rows: The cat crept **silently** across the roof.

blocks.title: Trap: -ly words that are adjectives
blocks.text: Not every -ly word is an adverb. *friendly, lovely, lonely, ugly, silly* are **adjectives**: *a **friendly** dog* (it describes the noun *dog*). And *fast* or *hard* can be both: *a **fast** car* (adjective) but *She ran **fast*** (adverb). Always ask: is it describing a **noun** (adjective) or a **verb/adjective** (adverb)?
6. Determiners
A **determiner** comes **before a noun** (and before any adjectives) and tells us **which one** or **how many**.

rows: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
some, many, much, few, a few, little, a little, every, each, all, no, several, any

blocks.text: **a or an?** Use **an** before a vowel **sound**: *an egg, an hour* (the h is silent). Use **a** before a consonant sound: *a cup, a university* (it sounds like "you").

**few / a few, little / a little:** *a few* and *a little* mean "some, enough", but *few* and *little* mean "not enough". *A few friends came* (good), but *Few friends came* (disappointing). Use *many / few* with countable nouns and *much / little* with uncountable nouns.

blocks.title: Determiner or pronoun?
blocks.text: If the word comes **before a noun**, it is a determiner: *"**This** bag is heavy."* If it stands **alone** instead of a noun, it is a pronoun: *"**This** is heavy."* The same goes for *my* (determiner: *my book*) and *mine* (pronoun: *The book is mine*).
7. Prepositions

A **preposition** shows the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and the rest of the sentence: **where** something is, **when** something happens, or **how**. A preposition is always followed by a noun or pronoun: *under **the bridge***, *after **lunch***, *with **her***.

rows: in, on, at, under, behind, between, beside, above, inside
to, into, across, through, towards, along, past
before, after, during, since, until, at, on, in
**During** the storm, the lights went out.
with, without, by, about, for, like, of
in April, in 2026, in the morning
on Monday, on 5th May, on my birthday
on the table, on the bus
at 7 o'clock, at night, at the weekend
at the door, at school, at home

blocks.title: Same word, different class
blocks.text: *before, after, since, until* can be **prepositions** or **conjunctions**. If a noun follows, it is a preposition: *after **lunch***. If a whole clause (with its own verb) follows, it is a conjunction: *after **we ate lunch***.
8. Conjunctions
A **conjunction** joins words, phrases or clauses.

rows: Coordinating conjunctions (join two equal parts) — remember **FANBOYS**
for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
I was hungry, **so** I made a sandwich.
Subordinating conjunctions (begin a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone)
because, although, when, while, if, unless, until, since, after, before, as, even though
**Although** it was raining, we played outside.

blocks.text: Conjunctions are explained fully on the **Connectives** page and in **Phrases and clauses**, because a subordinating conjunction is how a complex sentence is built.
9. Interjections

An **interjection** is a short word or phrase that shows a sudden feeling. It is often followed by an exclamation mark: *Ouch! Hooray! Oh no! Wow! Oops!* Interjections appear mostly in speech in stories.
Word class in context: the same word, different jobs
Checkpoint usually asks: *What is the word class of the word X **as it is used in this sentence**?* You cannot answer from the word alone. You must look at **what it is doing** in that sentence.

rows: We played **after** we finished our homework.
followed by a clause with a verb

blocks.text: **Four steps to name a word class in context:**

items: Find the word in the sentence and read the **whole** sentence.
Ask: is it **naming** something? (noun) Is it an **action or state**? (verb) Is it **describing a noun**? (adjective) Is it telling **how, when, where, how often** about a verb? (adverb)
Look at the **neighbours**. *The/a/my* before a word suggests a noun. A noun after it suggests a preposition or a determiner. *To* before a verb makes an infinitive.
Write the **exact name**: "adverb", not "describing word", and "abstract noun", not "noun" if the question asks for an abstract noun.

blocks.title: كيف تحدد نوع الكلمة في سؤال القراءة؟
items: لا تحكم على الكلمة من شكلها فقط؛ اقرأ الجملة كلها وانظر إلى وظيفة الكلمة فيها.
إذا جاءت قبلها a أو the فهي غالبًا اسم (noun)، وإذا كانت تصف اسمًا فهي صفة (adjective)، وإذا كانت تصف فعلًا (كيف، متى، أين) فهي ظرف (adverb).
to + فعل = infinitive، أما to + اسم = حرف جر (preposition).
who / which / that تكون relative pronoun فقط إذا جاءت بعد اسم وأعطت معلومات إضافية عنه.
اكتب المصطلح الإنجليزي بالضبط كما في السؤال، فالإجابة القريبة لا تأخذ درجة.

blocks.text: How Checkpoint asks about word classes
Here are typical question styles, written in our own words, with what a full-mark answer looks like.

rows: What word class is 'gently' as it is used in line 3?
Read the sentence and name the class.
Copy a relative pronoun from paragraph 2.
Find who / which / that / whose after a noun.
Find an abstract noun in the first paragraph.
Look for a feeling or idea word.
Write down an infinitive from the sentence.
Tick the word that is used as an adverb in the sentence.
Test each option: does it tell how/when/where?
Why does the writer use the modal verb 'must'?
To show that the action is necessary and urgent, which makes the advice sound strong.
Why does the writer use the comparative 'smaller'?
To compare the two rooms and show clearly that the new one has less space.

blocks.text: Practice A: name the word class
Read this short text, then answer the questions.

*Early on Saturday morning, Karim and his sister hurried to the harbour. The fishing boats, which had been out all night, were slowly returning. Karim felt a wave of excitement. "Look! That boat is the biggest," he shouted. His sister wanted to see the fishermen unload their nets.*

items.q: What word class is 'hurried'?
items.a: Verb. It is the action that Karim and his sister did.

items.q: What word class is 'slowly'?
items.a: Adverb (of manner). It tells us how the boats were returning.

items.q: Find an abstract noun in the text.
items.a: excitement. It is a feeling that you cannot touch or see.

items.q: Find a relative pronoun.
items.a: which ("The fishing boats, which had been out all night…"). It begins a relative clause that gives more information about the boats.

items.q: What word class is 'Saturday'? What type?
items.a: Noun: a proper noun (a day of the week, so it has a capital letter).

items.q: What word class is 'biggest'?
items.a: Adjective (superlative). It compares the boat with all the others.

items.q: Copy an infinitive from the text.
items.a: to see

items.q: What word class is 'Look!' here?
items.a: It is a verb used as a command (an imperative).

items.q: What word class is 'to' in 'hurried to the harbour'?
items.a: Preposition, because it is followed by a noun phrase (the harbour), not a verb.

items.q: What word class is 'their' in 'their nets'?
items.a: Determiner (possessive). It comes before the noun nets and shows whose nets.

items.q: What word class is 'That' in 'That boat is the biggest'?
items.a: Determiner (demonstrative), because it comes before the noun boat.

items.q: Find a proper noun that names a person.
items.a: Karim. It is the name of a particular person, so it starts with a capital letter.

blocks.text: Practice B: choose the correct answer

items.q: Which word is an abstract noun? (a) window (b) honesty (c) honest (d) teacher
items.a: (b) honesty. (c) honest is an adjective.

items.q: Which word is a modal verb? (a) should (b) quickly (c) because (d) under
items.a: (a) should.

items.q: In 'The man whose car broke down called for help', what is 'whose'?
items.a: A relative pronoun. It begins a relative clause about the man and shows the car belongs to him.

items.q: In 'She sings well', what word class is 'well'?
items.a: Adverb. It tells us how she sings.

items.q: In 'a lovely garden', what word class is 'lovely'?
items.a: Adjective. It ends in -ly but it describes the noun garden.

items.q: In 'We stayed inside until the rain stopped', what word class is 'until'?
items.a: Conjunction (subordinating), because it is followed by a clause with a verb: the rain stopped.

items.q: In 'We stayed inside until lunchtime', what word class is 'until'?
items.a: Preposition, because it is followed by a noun: lunchtime.

items.q: Make abstract nouns from: happy, enjoy, child, wise.
items.a: happiness, enjoyment, childhood, wisdom.

items.q: Which sentence uses 'that' as a relative pronoun? (a) That was close! (b) I know that you are right. (c) The cake that Gran made was delicious.
items.a: (c). That comes after the noun cake and tells us which cake.

items.q: Write the comparative and superlative of: good, careful, hot.
items.a: good → better → best, careful → more careful → most careful, hot → hotter → hottest.

items.q: Why might a writer use 'must' rather than 'could' in a leaflet about road safety?
items.a: 'Must' shows the action is necessary, not just possible, so the advice sounds serious and urgent and the reader is more likely to obey it.

items.q: Underline the determiners: 'Every child brought some bread and a bottle of water.'
items.a: Every, some, a.

blocks.text: Practice C: use word classes in your writing

items.q: Improve this sentence with a precise verb and an adverb: 'The dog went across the garden.'
items.a: Example: The dog bounded eagerly across the garden. (bounded = precise verb, eagerly = adverb of manner)

items.q: Add two adjectives to: 'The house stood at the end of the road.'
items.a: Example: The crumbling, silent house stood at the end of the road.

items.q: Rewrite with a relative clause: 'My uncle lives in Aswan. He is a doctor.'
items.a: My uncle, who lives in Aswan, is a doctor. (or: My uncle, who is a doctor, lives in Aswan.)

items.q: Write a sentence with an infinitive that shows purpose.
items.a: Example: Laila got up early to finish her painting before school.
